text:
Marathon Petroleum fell 2% today to $458.51, continuing a decline that started around October 21st. The sell-off comes despite oil prices climbing sharply—Brent crude hit $113 and U.S. crude sits at $107.89—driven by escalating Middle East tensions and Trump administration hints at strikes on Iran. For a refiner like this, rising crude costs eat into profits on fuel they produce, even though higher oil prices might seem bullish on the surface; refineries make money on the *spread* between what they pay for crude and what they receive for gasoline and diesel, and that margin shrinks when crude jumps faster than refined product prices catch up.

The broader pressure comes from a glut of refined products sitting in storage (205 million barrels of gasoline, 104 million barrels of diesel) paired with refineries running at 93% capacity—near full stretch with limited room to push through more volume. Meanwhile, geopolitical headlines hint at potential shifts in global refining power, including U.S. interest in Indian refining capacity to handle Venezuelan crude, which could fragment traditional supply chains that U.S. refiners have relied on.
